summary: East Point Lighthouse, Saturna Island, BC: first lit 1 January 1888, wooden tower replaced by a steel skeleton tower in 1948, unstaffed since 1996.

access.note: Parks Canada land at East Point Regional Park. Tower and grounds closed (LighthouseFriends). Reached by ferry to Saturna Island, then East Point Road.

events.note: Parliament appropriates money for a light on East Point; tenders are not called until after the John Rosenfeld wreck.
19 February 1886: the ship John Rosenfeld, in tow of the tug Tacoma, grounds on a reef near East Point.
John R. Wick, first keeper (LighthouseFriends roster; its text says just over a year).
Revolving white light first displayed 1 January 1888, focal plane 140 ft above high water (wooden tower).
14 June 1889: brush fire nearly consumes the new lighthouse while the keeper is away. Nephew George saves it; awarded $30.
Post light established on Patos Island, across Boundary Pass.
Tank shed built with three large tanks, $219.55.
Peter Georgeson succeeds his father James on his retirement.
February 1935: R. W. McMurray, President of the West Coast Steamship Service, petitions for a fog signal at East Point.
September 1937: experimental acetylene-powered fog gun installed in a small shack; often misfired.
Fog alarm building with diaphone horns constructed on the point.
Peter Georgeson transfers to Albert Head. Roster gives Henry Georgeson 1939-1940; the text says brother James kept the light that year. Unresolved.

Undated: one November between 1940 and 1960 the trawler Neptune II burst into flames passing the station. A U.S. Coast Guard crew took a man off the stern before it sank. Keeper's wife raised the alarm by radio.
Wooden tower replaced by a 14 m steel skeleton tower with a standard revolving beacon.
Nearby capture of the orca Moby Doll (Canadian Register).
Around 2006 the station is transferred to Parks Canada, to be added to the Gulf Islands National Park Reserve.

wrecks.outcome: Grounded on a reef near East Point while in tow of the tug Tacoma. Ship's back broken; sold for salvage. Coal from the wreck heated Saturna homes for years (LighthouseFriends).

American trawler, homebound from Alaska, burst into flames passing East Point. U.S. Coast Guard rescued a crewman from the stern before the vessel sank. Undated in the source; the keeper was Andrew Ritchie (1940-1960).

notes_for_editor: Checked 2026-10-27. Page images were read for the keepers' tables: 1902 p. 70 and 1907 p. 148 print 'Georgeson, James' beside 'Saturna Island, East Point' (the 1902 and 1907 reading holds); 1912 p. 74 prints 'Saturna island' as the station beside 'J. Georgeson' (appointed 26 Oct 1889), with no East Point, so the story does not put East Point in 1912. The 1924 (p. 135) and 1925 (p. 125) printed pages are confirmed by the corpus OCR heads (no '?'). Those two reports are named by the year they were printed, because their fiscal-year label was not confirmed here. The Argus (25 Feb 1886 p. 3) and the Daily Morning Astorian (26 Feb 1886 p. 3) were read; the Argus says the tide was high and began to fall, and the Astorian says the wreck would be sold next Monday in Victoria. The Canadian Register statement was read; its phrasing is quoted as printed. The Register says the light was established following the wreck; LighthouseFriends says Parliament appropriated money in 1885, before the wreck. Both are stated. LighthouseFriends conflicts: John R. Wick's span (roster 1886-1889; text 'just over a year'); Henry Georgeson (roster 1939-1940) against 'his brother James' (text, same years), which the story leaves open. Neptune II: LighthouseFriends does not give the year; the story says so. The keeper's wife's radio call is in LighthouseFriends without a name; the story names no one there. Named keepers after 1960: none. Andrew Ritchie (retired 1960) is named only in the published roster span. Peter Fletcher, Ian G. McNeil and Arthur G. Walden appear only in the roster in the research file. Excluded on purpose: LighthouseFriends' oral-history anecdotes (the skull fragments, the Skookum Tom recollection, the keeper's wife's water remarks) and the Marine reports' East Point entries for other stations. The Argus OCR garbles the 'Tumbo' island name; not quoted. Record items not supported by any source read: 'Fl W 15s' and focal height 36.9 m (unverified); the 2013 designation (unverified here). The Parks Canada DFHD page (id 14514) returned only a site frame. No photos mirrored.
